title: Is Teleworking Sustainable?

paragraphs.text: The research study was created in 2002 by the European Union’s Information Society Technologies Programme. The aim of the research study was to examine the influence of telework (i.e. working from home) on sustainable development by assessing its economic, environmental and social impacts. Researchers from the UK Centre for Economic and Environmental Development gathered data and analysed 40 case studies and survey data from seven different types of organisations (from public administration to insurers to IT) in five countries (Denmark, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands and the UK).

Economically, the benefits of better work performance, reduced absenteeism and improved recruitment and retention associated with telework were validated by the study. Two case studies allowed direct comparisons of productivity between teleworkers and non-teleworkers and found an increase among teleworkers in productivity, along with reduced absenteeism and increased job satisfaction. Other factors that contributed to higher work performance included better quality, higher output and greater creativity. Telework increases business resilience, since it allows work to be done when building operations are disrupted by factors such as the weather, but the report cautions that it also makes the organisation more vulnerable to disruption of information systems (such as intranets).

The influence of telework on human capital development (the personal competencies and skills needed to create wealth) was mostly positive, with the exception being one organisation in which a large minority of the respondents saw a negative effect on career development. Seven of the studies found that telework had a significantly positive effect on internal communication and knowledge sharing, often due to the conscious implementation of technological tools during telework programme deployment. At the individual level, the main financial benefit of telework was reduced commuting costs, which almost all respondents saw as outweighing the increased cost of energy in their home.

In the past, traditional forms of telework were seen as having negative effects on the demands on energy and equipment in the home, unless reductions in office building-related energy consumption were attained. Respondents in the case studies were split on whether telework increased or decreased paper usage, but extensive use of a company intranet was linked to significant reductions in teleworkers’ use of their printers, since information could be sent electronically to colleagues and consulted on screen.

The commuting ‘rebound effect’ associated with telework, if any, has been the topic of considerable discussion. In other words, are reductions in commute miles (and thus air pollution) offset by increased miles driven for such routine tasks as shopping, for instance, or because cars previously used for commuting are now available for other purposes? Researchers found that telework is indeed significantly reducing travel even when these offsetting factors are taken into account. However, mobile teleworkers (in sales, for example) were more likely to replace the trip into the office with trips to other work-related places.

In the social dimension, the study clearly validates the connection between telework and good quality of life. Many respondents missed the human interaction at the office, but a greater ability to concentrate showed up in improved work performance. The apparent paradox between longer working hours and improved quality of life is explained by the even greater time saved by not commuting, reduced stress and better ability to manage the various demands on a person’s time. (An unmentioned factor might be the link between job performance and job satisfaction, and between job satisfaction and quality of life.) The study was unable to distinguish between telework and general environmental factors such as company culture or competition as causes of the longer working hours. However, the study found that telework does change the pattern of work – most respondents reported flexible work patterns that at times resulted in them beginning work earlier in the morning and/or ending later in the evenings, having taken longer breaks during the day.

Various studies have found that teleworkers take fewer sick days, but is this because they simply work when they are sick? Interestingly, a large number of respondents in all countries felt that telework actually had a beneficial effect on their health, due to factors such as reduced stress, less driving, more exercise and better diet. A good number also reported that teleworking made it easier for them to be involved in organised local community activities.

To sum up, while the research considered a number of potentially negative effects of telework, it found that these effects can be minimised by proper programme management and are outweighed by many more potentially positive effects for staff working at home. The researchers conclude that ‘well-managed teleworking schemes which recognise, and seek to minimise, negative impacts should be accepted as sustainable unless there is clear evidence to the contrary’.
